Most Starsim models run fast with no help: a compartmental model of a year in daily steps reruns in under a millisecond, and agents take time in proportion to the number of agents and steps. When a run is slower than that, it is nearly always for one of a few reasons, and the first half of this page covers how to find them and what to do. How the solvers and backends work is in [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd).

A study with thousands of runs, or a model that others use through a web page, needs more than a laptop and a notebook. Starsim is plain Python, so it runs anywhere Python does: on one large computer, on a cluster, or behind a dashboard. The second half of this page covers moving an analysis from a notebook into a script, and then each of these. Making many sims and comparing them is in [Scenarios](running_scenarios.qmd); this page is about how fast they run, and where.

```{python}
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.1, 0.5])
sir = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ beta*I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(10), init_n=dict(I=100), name='sir')
pars = dict(total_pop=1_000_000, start='2026-01-01', stop='2026-12-31', dt=ss.days(1), solver='ode', verbose=0)
```

## A compartmental run in one call

A compartmental run is fastest when the compiled kernels can take every step in one call, with nothing in Python between the steps. Anything that needs Python at each step takes the run a step at a time, which is typically 30 to 100 times slower. The `plan` line of `sim.describe()` says whether a run is taken in one call, and if not, why (a run says so too, as it starts):

```{python}
masks = ss.modify(sir.pars.beta, multiply=0.75, who=sir.I.n >= 20_000) # Fewer contacts while prevalence is high
late = ss.modify(sir.pars.beta, multiply=0.75, who=sir.I.n >= 20_000, until=sir.I.n <= 10_000) # As above, ending at a lower level
for mod in [masks, late]:
    plan = [line for line in ss.Sim(sir, interventions=mod, **pars).describe().splitlines() if 'plan' in line]
    print(plan[0].strip())
```

The first runs in one call: a condition on a count is worked out within the kernels as part of the rate. The second needs to remember whether the measure is on, so it is taken a step at a time. To be told rather than slowed, give the sim `require_kernels=True`: a run that would fall back to Python then raises `ss.CapabilityError`, with the reason.

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(sir, interventions=masks, require_kernels=True, **pars).run() # Fine: the whole run is in the kernels
```

What stays in the kernels, and what does not:

| In the kernels | A step at a time |
|---|---|
| Parameters that vary in time (`ss.timeseries`, `ss.seasonal`) | A parameter that is a function of the sim (`lambda sim: ...`), called at each step |
| `ss.modify()` with `when=` (a window, `ss.schedule(start=, stop=)`, other times, or a function of the date), `who=` on a stratum (or on a state, for a transition), or `who=` comparing the module's counts (`I.n >= 1000`) | `ss.modify()` with `until=`, a function as its amount, `who=` as a function of the sim, or `who=` on incidence over a period (`infection.incidence(over=ss.days(7))`) |
| Deliveries such as `ss.vaccinate()` at fixed times or on a schedule, including coverage given as a rate (`ss.peryear(0.5)`) | Deliveries with `who=` on a count, and `ss.treat()` |
| Outcomes, including those with a delay | Triggers (`ss.on(...)`) |
| Births and deaths declared with `ss.birth()` and `ss.death()` | Interventions, analyzers, or connectors written as code with a `step()` of their own |
| `verbose=0` or `1` | `verbose=2`, `until=` in `sim.run()`, `sim.profile(kind='loop')`, and diagnostics |

A module written as code is always taken a step at a time, since its `step()` is Python. If it only needs to act at a few times, or on a condition that one of the declared forms above can say, writing it that way keeps the run in the kernels.

## Many runs

Running the same model many times is fastest with `ss.parallel()`: with `n_runs=`, `pars=`, or `priors=`, a sim that runs in one call is built once, and all its runs are taken together by the kernels. A loop that builds each sim again, such as `[sim.new(rand_seed=i).run() for i in range(100)]`, rebuilds the model each time, which takes about 10 milliseconds, many times the run itself.

```{python}
msim = ss.parallel(ss.Sim(sir, **pars), pars=dict(beta=[0.2, 0.3, 0.4]), n_runs=10, workers=1) # 30 runs, taken together
```

For the same reason, rerun a sim with `sim.run()` again (or `sim.restart(pars=...).run()` for new values) rather than `sim.new()`, unless the model itself has changed. Fitting does this already.

## Substeps

The ODE and the chain binomial take as many substeps in each time step as they need, by default: enough that no compartment turns over by more than a quarter in one. Working out how many costs about as much as a substep itself. `ss.solvers.ode(substeps=1)` or `ss.solvers.binomial(substeps=1)` takes each step whole: it changes the results by an amount that grows with the step (of order the rates times `dt`), so it suits models whose rates are slow compared with the step, and models that are written in discrete time. It makes little difference to the kernels, but a run in JAX takes about half the time.

## JAX and gradients

How Starsim chooses between the kernels and JAX is in [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd#backends). On a CPU, a small model is faster in the kernels: a run of a year of an SIR in daily steps takes about 0.3 ms in the kernels and about 18 ms in JAX, since JAX's cost for each step of a loop dominates when each step is a handful of numbers. JAX gains on large models, on a GPU, and on many runs at once. A run is taken by the kernels unless `sim.jax = True`; gradients and many runs at once use JAX by themselves. For a fit, `method='nelder-mead'` works with the kernels alone, and is chosen by default for one or two fitted parameters; L-BFGS-B uses gradients from JAX.

## Agents

An agent-based run takes time in proportion to the number of agents and the number of steps. For speed:

- **Use fewer agents than people.** `total_pop=` with a smaller `n_agents=` lets each agent stand for several people (see [Branching and rescaling](running_branching.qmd)).
- **Use compartments if nothing needs individuals.** If a model needs no network, no per-person values, and no histories, `solver='ode'` or a stochastic compartmental solver is far faster at any population size.
- **Threads.** The passes over the agents of a large sim (more than about 200,000 agents) use several threads; `ss.options.threads` sets how many, and `ss.options.blas_threads` the threads of NumPy's linear algebra. When running many sims at once on one machine, one thread each (`SCIRIS_NUM_THREADS=1`) avoids them competing for the cores (see [One level of parallelism](#on-a-cluster-with-a-job-scheduler)).
- **Common random numbers.** `ss.options.crn = False` gives faster draws, at the cost of runs no longer matching across scenarios agent for agent (see [Random numbers](mechanics_random.qmd)).

## Code of your own

A module written as code runs its `step()` in Python, once a step. Starsim then stays out of the way: a compartmental model written as a module that holds its own numbers runs a year of daily steps in about a millisecond, about as fast as the same model declared, though it can't be taken in one call to the kernels, run in JAX, or differentiated. What decides the speed of your own code is how it handles the people.

- **Work on arrays, not people.** A loop over the agents in Python is many times slower than the same work on the whole array at once (see [Array indexing](mechanics_indexing.qmd)).
- **Compile a loop that can't be written as array operations.** `@ss.jit` compiles a function with Numba, keeps it on disk between sessions, and says why if it can't (see [Custom modules](building_modules.qmd)). Called with JAX arrays, the same function is traced by JAX instead, so it can be differentiated. A function compiled with Numba's own `@nb.njit` works as well, and is as fast.
- **Compiled code is compatible with either set of kernels.** Your functions are compiled with Numba whether Starsim's own kernels are Rust or Numba, and the two don't interact: Starsim passes NumPy arrays to your code, and takes NumPy arrays back.
- **Draw random numbers from Starsim's distributions** (`ss.bernoulli`, `ss.normal`, and the others) rather than `np.random`, so that runs stay reproducible and scenarios share their random numbers (see [Random numbers](mechanics_random.qmd)); their draws are compiled already.

As an example, a module that updates a value for each of 50,000 agents at each step, run for 20 steps alongside an SIR on a random network:

| How the update is written | Whole run |
|---|---|
| A loop over the agents in Python | 0.38 s |
| NumPy operations on the whole array | 0.073 s |
| The same loop, with `@ss.jit` | 0.062 s |
| The same loop, with `@nb.njit` | 0.058 s |
| No such module | 0.053 s |

The compiled loop costs about a tenth of the rest of the run, close to what Starsim's own compiled code would take for the same work. Fused kernels are faster still for a compartmental model, since the whole run is one call, but for agents most of the time is in the network and the disease, which are compiled already.

## Finding where the time goes

`sim.profile(kind='loop')` records how long each part of each step takes, and `sim.profile()` how long each line of a function takes; [Profiling and debugging](running_debugging.qmd#profiling) shows how to use them. Profiling takes the run a step at a time, so use it to find the slow part, not to time the run; `sim.elapsed` gives the seconds of the last run.

## Compiling first

If a first run after installing is slow, the Numba kernels are being compiled; `ss.compile()` (or `starsim init compile`) does it once ahead of time (see [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd#backends)). This matters most on a cluster, where hundreds of tasks would otherwise each compile it, or wait for each other to (see [below](#on-a-cluster-with-a-job-scheduler)).

## From a notebook to a script

An analysis that will be run again (by you next month, by a colleague, or on another computer) is best kept as a script rather than a notebook: inputs explicit, the model made by a function, and the results saved with what is needed to make them again. A script that runs sims in parallel puts the work under `if __name__ == '__main__':`, so that the worker processes, which import the script, don't start the analysis again (this is required on Windows and macOS):

```python
# measles_campaign.py
import sciris as sc
import starsim as ss

def make_sim(coverage=0.5, seed=1):
    """ The measles model, with a campaign on day 30 """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    beta = ss.par(1.9)
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=5))
    campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, when=ss.days(30), coverage=coverage)
    return ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180),
                  solver='binomial', rand_seed=seed, label=f'Coverage {coverage}', verbose=0)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    sims = [make_sim(coverage) for coverage in [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75]]
    msim = ss.parallel(sims, n_runs=100)
    msim.to_df(quantiles=[0.025, 0.5, 0.975]).to_csv('measles_campaign.csv', index=False)  # The results, as quantiles over the runs
    sc.savejson('measles_campaign_info.json', dict(            # What is needed to make them again
        starsim = ss.__version__,
        git = sc.gitinfo(__file__),
        date = sc.getdate(),
    ))
```

Keep the computation and the presentation apart: a script (or a cluster job) saves tables, and a notebook makes the figures from them, so a figure can be changed without running everything again. Record the version of Starsim and of your own code (`sc.gitinfo()` gives the commit), the data, the seeds, and the parameter values; a saved table with these is reproducible long after a saved sim (a pickle, which needs the same versions of the code to load) has stopped loading. Check one run and one small batch before a large one.

## On one large computer

The simplest way to run more is a larger computer, such as a cloud virtual machine with many cores. `ss.parallel()` already runs sims on all the cores of the computer it is on, so a script that uses it needs no changes. Here, the measles model is run for ten values of β, ten times each:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import sciris as sc
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=5)) # 90% immune, 5 infectious

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), solver='binomial', verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(beta=np.linspace(1.5, 2.3, 10)), n_runs=10)
msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']
```

`workers=` limits the number of cores used (for a shared computer), and `workers=1` runs the sims one after another in this process, which is useful for debugging, since an error then comes with its full traceback.

When the sims differ in more than parameter values, make them in a loop, or with a function (see [Running sims](running_sim.qmd#larger-projects-make_sim)), and give the list to `ss.parallel()`. If making each sim is itself slow (reading large data files, or building a large population), make them in parallel too, with `sc.parallelize()` from Sciris:

```{python}
def make_sim(seed, coverage):
    campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, when=ss.days(30), coverage=coverage)
    return ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), solver='binomial', rand_seed=seed, label='Campaign', verbose=0)

sims = sc.parallelize(make_sim, iterarg=range(1, 9), coverage=0.5) # One sim for each seed, 1 to 8
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

Making sims in parallel copies each one back to the main process, which takes time for a large sim; `sc.parallelize(..., serial=True)` makes them one after another, to check whether parallel is faster. Since the eight sims have the same label, they are runs of one scenario, and the plot shows their median and spread; sims with different labels are scenarios of their own (and so is each sim with no label).

::: {.callout-tip}
A remote computer can be used through SSH and a terminal, or from an editor on your own computer: [VS Code](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-vscode-remote.remote-ssh) (and editors based on it, such as [Positron](https://positron.posit.co)), [PyCharm](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/pycharm/configuring-remote-interpreters-via-ssh.html), and [Spyder](https://docs.spyder-ide.org/current/panes/ipythonconsole.html#connect-to-a-remote-kernel) all connect to a remote Python. A Jupyter server on the remote computer (such as [The Littlest JupyterHub](https://tljh.jupyter.org/)) works too.
:::

### Threads for linear algebra

NumPy and SciPy do their linear algebra with a library called BLAS, which can use many threads. Starsim sets it to one thread when it is imported: on the machines we tested, more threads didn't make Starsim faster, and they slow down starting up and starting workers. More threads can speed up large matrix calculations of your own, so you can change this:

```python
ss.options.blas_threads = 4 # For the rest of the session; use 0 to leave BLAS as it is

with ss.options.context(blas_threads=4): # Or just for this block
    results = my_matrix_calculation()
```

Or set it from the shell, with `STARSIM_BLAS_THREADS=4 python my_script.py`. This is separate from `ss.options.threads` (`STARSIM_THREADS`), which sets the threads for Starsim's own loops over agents.

On Linux, this works at any time. On Windows and macOS, it can't change BLAS once NumPy has been imported, though workers of `ss.parallel()` still get it. This rarely matters, but if it does, import Starsim before NumPy, or set `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS` (`VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS` on a Mac) before starting Python.

## On a cluster with Dask

For more runs than one computer can manage, tools such as [Dask](https://docs.dask.org/) spread them across many computers. Each task makes and runs a sim and returns it; `sim.shrink()` first removes the people, so that only the results are sent back. `ss.MultiSim()` then collects sims that have already run, without running them again. (This and the next example are not run on this page.)

```python
import dask
import dask.distributed as dd
import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

def run_sim(seed, beta):
    """ Make and run one sim, and return it without its people """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=5))
    sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), solver='binomial', rand_seed=seed, label=f'beta={beta}', verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    sim.shrink()
    return sim

if __name__ == '__main__':
    client = dd.Client(n_workers=4)
    tasks = [dask.delayed(run_sim)(seed, beta) for seed in range(1, 11) for beta in [1.5, 1.9, 2.3]]
    sims = list(dask.compute(*tasks))
    msim = ss.MultiSim(sims) # Collects the results of sims that have run
    msim.plot()
```

[Coiled](https://coiled.io/), a paid service built on Dask, runs the same tasks on a cluster in the cloud that grows and shrinks with the work:

```python
import coiled

cluster = coiled.Cluster(n_workers=50, workspace='<your_coiled_workspace>')
client = cluster.get_client()
futures = [client.submit(run_sim, seed, 1.9) for seed in range(1, 1001)]
sims = client.gather(futures)
msim = ss.MultiSim(sims)
msim.plot()
```

Dask's workers set `MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_` so that freed memory goes back to the system at once, which slows sims down by making them fault in new pages. On Linux with glibc, importing Starsim overrides this, so nothing needs to be set; a task that needs that memory back during a long job can call `ss.solvers.backends.release_memory()`.

The same pattern (a function that makes, runs, and shrinks one sim, given a seed and the values that differ) works with other tools, such as [Joblib](https://joblib.readthedocs.io/).

## On a cluster with a job scheduler

On a high-performance cluster run by a scheduler such as [Slurm](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html), the usual pattern is a job array: the same script is run many times, each with its own task number, which picks the seed and the scenario. Each job saves its sim (shrunk) or, better, a table of the results it needs, and a final script collects them:

```python
# run_one.py: run as one task of a job array, e.g. with sbatch --array=0-399
import os
import starsim as ss
from measles_campaign import make_sim

task = int(os.environ['SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID'])
coverages = [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75]
coverage, seed = coverages[task % 4], task // 4 + 1  # 100 seeds of each of 4 scenarios
sim = make_sim(coverage=coverage, seed=seed)
sim.run()
sim.save(f'results/sim_{task}.sim')  # Shrunk by default, since it has finished
```

```python
# collect.py: once every task has finished
import glob
import starsim as ss

sims = [ss.load(filename) for filename in sorted(glob.glob('results/sim_*.sim'))]
msim = ss.MultiSim(sims)  # Collects sims that have already run; sims with the same label are runs of one scenario
msim.summarize()
```

Three things matter more on a cluster than on a laptop:

- **One level of parallelism.** When the scheduler already runs many tasks at once, don't have each task start a pool of its own: use `ss.parallel(..., workers=1)` within a task, or limit it with `workers=`. Within one sim, Starsim uses several threads only for passes over very large populations (200,000 agents or more), and never in the workers of `ss.parallel()`; `ss.options.threads = 1` (or the environment variable `STARSIM_THREADS=1`) turns them off. NumPy's linear algebra (OpenBLAS or MKL) has threads of its own, which the workers of `ss.parallel()` divide among themselves; to keep them to one, set `SCIRIS_NUM_THREADS=1` in the task's environment (e.g. in the job script), or call `sc.limit_threads(1)`. None of these limits the Numba threads that Starsim's passes use; `STARSIM_THREADS=1` does.
- **Compile once, before the runs.** Starsim's compiled code (see [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd#backends)) is compiled on first use and kept on disk. Run `starsim init compile` (or `ss.compile()`) once after installing, in the shared environment or when building a container image, so that hundreds of tasks don't each compile it, or wait for each other to; `starsim init compile --check` says whether it has been done. `starsim init` compiles too, and also installs the skills for AI coding agents (see the [appendix](#appendix-the-starsim-command)).
- **Settings from the environment.** Every option in `ss.options` can be set by an environment variable, `STARSIM_` and its name in capitals (`STARSIM_THREADS=1`, `STARSIM_VERBOSE=0`, `STARSIM_WARNINGS=error`), which is the easiest way to set it for every task of a job; the full list, with each variable, is in the [appendix](#appendix-every-option).
- **The same code everywhere.** Install the same versions of Starsim and of your own modules on every node (a container image, or a shared environment), since a saved sim needs them to load.

## Interactive dashboards

A model can be put behind a web page, so that others can change its inputs and see the results. There are several tools for this, including [Shiny for Python](https://shiny.posit.co/py/), [Voilà](https://voila.readthedocs.io/), and [Panel](https://panel.holoviz.org/); one of the simplest is [Streamlit](https://streamlit.io/). This one has sliders for the share of the town that is immune and the coverage of a vaccination campaign:

```python
import streamlit as st
import starsim as ss

def run_sim(immune, coverage):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=immune), init_n=dict(I=5))
    campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, when=ss.days(30), coverage=coverage)
    sim = ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    return sim

st.title('Measles in a town of 20,000')
immune = st.slider('Share immune at the start', 0.5, 0.99, 0.9)
coverage = st.slider('Coverage of the campaign on day 30', 0.0, 1.0, 0.5)

sim = run_sim(immune, coverage)
st.write('Infections:', round(sim.results.measles.infection.sum()))
st.pyplot(sim.diseases.measles.plot())
```

Saved as `app.py`, it runs (after `pip install streamlit`) with `streamlit run app.py`, which opens the dashboard in a browser. As an ODE, each run takes a fraction of a second, so the page updates as the sliders move.

## Pitfalls

- **Sending whole sims between computers.** A sim with its people can be large; shrink it before returning it (`sim.shrink()`), as `ss.parallel()` does by itself.
- **The same seed in every task.** Give each run its own `rand_seed`, or every run of a stochastic model is the same.
- **Workers that compete for cores.** A pool of processes in each of many tasks on one node runs slower than one; use one level of parallelism.
- **Code that isn't on the workers.** A module written as code must be importable on every computer that runs it, since sims are sent between them as Python objects (pickles), which need the same code to be read.

- [Slurm: Job arrays](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html): running the same script many times with a task number

## Appendix: every option

Starsim's global options are in `ss.options`: set one for the session with `ss.options(threads=1)`, for a block with `with ss.options(threads=1):`, or before Python starts with the environment variable `STARSIM_` and the option's name in capitals (`STARSIM_THREADS=1`), which is the way to set it for every worker or every task of a cluster job. `ss.options.disp()` shows the current values, and `ss.options.help(detailed=True)` each option's value, default, and variable. Here is each option with its description:

```{python}
import pandas as pd
pd.set_option('display.max_colwidth', None) # Show each entry in full

rows = {key: dict(variable=f'STARSIM_{key.upper()}', description=ss.options.optdesc[key]) for key in ss.options.keys()}
pd.DataFrame.from_dict(rows, orient='index')
```

Those that affect speed or memory are `threads` and `blas_threads` (threads for the agents and for linear algebra), `kernels` and `jax` (which code runs the solvers; see [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd#appendix-every-set-of-kernels)), `crn` (faster draws for agents, without common random numbers), `keep_times` and `max_joint` (memory), `precision` (32, the default, keeps agents' values as 32-bit floats, and 64 as 64-bit, which doubles their memory), and `max_steps` (when to warn that a run has many steps); `max_years` (1,000 by default) says when to warn that a run is so long it is probably a mistake. Starsim also reads `SCIRIS_NUM_THREADS`, as it reads `STARSIM_BLAS_THREADS`, for the threads of linear algebra (see [Threads for linear algebra](#threads-for-linear-algebra)), and `STARSIM_CHECK_COUNTS` and `STARSIM_CHECK_DRAWS`, which turn on checks of the agent engine for testing it, at a cost in speed.

The settings of a sim that affect speed or memory are `n_agents` and `total_pop` (whose ratio is the people each agent stands for), `dt`, `solver` (and its `substeps=`), `require_kernels`, `group_results` (which results are kept by group), and `record_people` (whether the people's results are recorded at each step); they are all in [Running sims](running_sim.qmd#appendix-every-sim-setting). The rules that decide whether a compartmental run is taken in one call are in [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd#appendix-what-needs-agents), as `ss.solvers.solver_table()`.

## Appendix: the starsim command

Installing Starsim also installs a `starsim` command, for setting up an environment and converting models (`starsim` lists these, and `starsim <command> --help` the options of each):

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `starsim init` | Once, after installing: `starsim init ai` if an AI coding agent is installed, then `starsim init compile` unless the Rust kernels are in use (`-y` not to ask anything) |
| `starsim init compile` | Compiles the Numba kernels ahead of time, as `ss.compile()` does (once per install; a few minutes). Optional: they are otherwise compiled on first use, and with the Rust kernels in use (as from the wheels on PyPI) they are needed only to compare the two |
| `starsim init compile --rust` | In a clone of Starsim, builds the Rust kernels instead, installing Rust first if it is missing. Without `--rust` (or `--numba`), a clone whose Rust kernels are not built is asked which to do |
| `starsim init compile --check` | Says which kernels are in use and whether they are compiled, and exits with 1 if not (for a build script) |
| `starsim init ai` | Links the Starsim skills for AI coding agents into this project, after asking (`-y` not to ask), as `starsim ai install` does. `--global` installs a short skill for all projects instead, `--to=claude,agents` chooses the agents (by default, each one installed), and `--force` replaces a skill of the same name that `starsim` did not install; `starsim init` and `starsim init dev` take these too |
| `starsim init dev` | For a clone of Starsim: also the development dependencies, Rust if it is missing, and both sets of kernels |
| `starsim ai` | Where the skills are installed (as `starsim ai status` says) |
| `starsim ai list` | Lists the skills, with what each is for |
| `starsim ai show` | Shows the guide for AI agents, which lists the skills, or one skill (`starsim ai show convert-model`) |
| `starsim ai install` | Links the skills into this project, as `starsim init ai` does, with the same options; `starsim ai uninstall` removes them (`--global`: the short skill for all projects) |
| `starsim ai off` | Stops the other `starsim` commands from suggesting the skills; `starsim ai on` lets them again |
| `starsim convert model.R` | Converts a model to Starsim code (`model.py`), telling the format from the file (or as `--from=` says); `--to=` another format, `--out=` the file, and `--force` to replace it if it exists. `starsim convert` lists the formats |
| `starsim convert laser_model.py --ai` | Has an AI coding agent do the conversion, with Starsim's skills, in an interactive session (`--headless` to run it on its own). `--ai=claude` names the agent; by default, it is the one in the `STARSIM_AGENT` environment variable, or else the only one installed |
| `starsim import model.camdl` | The same as `starsim convert model.camdl --to=starsim`; a second argument gives the format, if it can't be told from the file (`starsim import model.json epipack`) |
| `starsim import sir.xlsx atomica --databook=data.xlsx` | When importing, any other option goes to the importer, as a keyword argument of `ss.import_from()` (here, `databook='data.xlsx'`) |
| `starsim export model.py sbml` | Writes the sim that `model.py` makes (as `sim`, or `--sim=`) in another format |
| `starsim --version` | The version of Starsim |
